article.title: Selection Bias in Machine-Learning Campaigns
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Machine-learning campaigns often compare the conversion rate of customers selected by a model with the conversion rate of a random group. If the model-selected group converts more often, teams may say that the model created the improvement. That conclusion can be wrong because the groups were selected differently before the campaign began. A propensity model is designed to identify customers who already have characteristics associated with a higher probability of conversion. If the top-scoring customers are contacted while a random sample represents the full population, the two groups have different baseline risk. A higher observed conversion rate among model-selected customers can therefore reflect selection rather than incremental campaign impact. This is selection bias. The distinction matters because targeting and causal effect answer different questions. A model may be excellent at finding people who will purchase, yet many of those people might purchase without receiving the message. For resource allocation, the business may instead care about customers whose behavior can be changed by the intervention. A clean experimental design separates selection from treatment. One approach is to define the target population first and then randomly assign treatment and control within that same population. If the objective is to evaluate a model-based targeting strategy against random targeting, the design must ensure that the comparison represents the strategies fairly and that exposure rules are clear. Stratification can help maintain balance on important pre-treatment variables. Analysis should also distinguish response rate, incremental lift, and total incremental conversions. A high response rate among selected customers is valuable for operational efficiency, but it is not automatically evidence of causal lift. Propensity scores can also be used in observational causal methods, but that use is different from using a predictive propensity model for ranking. Matching or weighting requires assumptions about measured confounders and overlap. It does not magically turn every model score into a causal estimate. Leakage creates another form of misleading selection if features contain information recorded after the decision point. Such a model may look powerful offline but cannot reproduce the same ranking at deployment. Analysts should document the eligible population, scoring time, feature availability, selection rule, treatment assignment, control construction, and outcome window. When presenting results, say “the model-selected population had a higher observed conversion rate” unless the design supports a stronger causal statement. To claim that model-based targeting improved outcomes, estimate what would have happened under an appropriate alternative strategy. Selection is often the purpose of predictive modeling, but selection itself changes the population being measured. Evaluation must account for that change rather than treating every difference in conversion as treatment effect. Analysts should state the population, observation window, assumptions, and decision point before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed pattern from the mechanism that may have produced it and from the action that should follow. This discipline makes the analysis easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate to stakeholders. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文重點是不要讓單一摘要數字、留下來的樣本、模型選擇結果或統計調整取代對資料生成機制的理解。分析時要先界定母體、時間點、selection mechanism 與真正要回答的 business question，再判斷觀察到的差異可以支持到什麼程度。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：単一の要約値、生き残ったsample、modelによるselection、統計的な調整だけでdata generating processを置き換えて考えないことが重要である。母集団、時点、selection mechanism、business questionを先に定義し、観察された差がどこまでの結論を支持できるかを判断する。
